pairs.rationale: Both urge submission to governing authorities for a God-oriented reason. Peter names king and governors and says submission is for the Lord's sake; Romans explicitly grounds the existing authorities in God's appointment.

The stated conclusion about resisting God's ordering follows the preceding premise that existing authorities have been appointed by God. This is the letter's own premise-and-consequence argument, rather than an independent narrative about a particular ruler.
Both describe the public authority's contrasting response to evil and good: punishment of evildoers and praise of those doing good. Romans develops that contrast through the question about fear.

The earlier prohibition reserves repayment to the Lord; this verse describes an authority as God's avenger for wrath. The comparison follows vengeance and wrath language while distinguishing private retaliation from the described public role.

Romans adds conscience to the motive of avoiding wrath. Peter describes enduring unjust sorrows out of awareness of God. The shared God-facing motive is compared while retaining Peter's different immediate setting of household slaves and masters.

Both connect payment of tribute or taxes with obligation under God. Romans describes the authorities as God's ministers; Jesus answers the tribute question by distinguishing rendering Caesar's things and God's things.

Both list owed honor and fear in a context that includes public authority. Peter specifically assigns fear to God and honor to the king; Romans lists the respective dues without naming each recipient.
Both make love of another or neighbor the fulfillment of law. Galatians explicitly cites the neighbor-love saying; Romans introduces that principle through the continuing obligation to love.

Paul's four prohibitions correspond to adultery, murder, theft and coveting in the Decalogue. The pinned Greek-order Exodus places theft before murder and includes false witness in this span; Romans does not reproduce that intervening command.
Romans quotes the command to love one's neighbor as oneself as the summary of the prohibitions. Leviticus gives that command alongside the prohibition of vengeance and continued anger.

Romans says love does no evil to the neighbor. Corinthians describes love as not seeking its own interests, not keeping account of wrong and not rejoicing in unrighteousness; it expands love's conduct without repeating the law-fulfillment formulation.

Both join the approaching day with ethical wakefulness and salvation. Thessalonians develops light, day, vigilance and the hope of salvation; it does not repeat Romans's comparison with the time when believers first believed.

Both contrast day and light with night and darkness and use putting-on imagery for readiness. Romans names weapons of light; Thessalonians specifies a breastplate of faith and love and a helmet of salvation's hope.

The vice lists overlap specifically in licentiousness, strife, jealousy, drunkenness and revelries, alongside sexual wrongdoing. Romans contrasts this conduct with honorable daytime living; Galatians calls its catalogue works of the flesh.
Both use the distinctive image of putting on Christ. Galatians relates it to baptism into Christ; Romans uses it as an exhortation and adds the rejection of provision for fleshly desires.

The later instruction repeats welcoming one another and grounds it in Christ's welcome. It develops the present instruction to welcome the person weak in faith without turning reception into disputes over opinions.

Both discuss weakness in connection with eating or abstaining. Romans names vegetables and weak faith; Corinthians names idol-associated food and a weak conscience. This does not identify the groups or supply an unstated reason for Roman abstinence.
Both reject judging people over eating. Romans addresses reciprocal contempt and judgment between eaters and abstainers whom God welcomes; Colossians also includes drinking and calendar observances.

Both challenge judging a brother or neighbor by asking who the human judge is in relation to the Lord's authority. Romans uses another master's household slave and the Lord's ability to make him stand; James names the one Lawgiver and Judge.

Both discuss religious distinctions involving days. Romans contrasts regarding one day and regarding all alike and requires personal conviction; Colossians warns against judgment over festival, new moon or Sabbaths and calls them a shadow.

Both connect eating with thanksgiving and a God-directed purpose. Romans also includes abstaining and regarding a day for the Lord; Corinthians speaks of thankful participation and doing eating, drinking and all else for God's glory.

Romans denies that believers live for themselves. Corinthians similarly says those who live should no longer live for themselves but for the One who died and was raised; Romans additionally includes dying in its statement.

Romans says believers belong to the Lord whether living or dying. Corinthians says they are not their own because they were bought at a price and therefore should glorify God in the body; the common point is belonging rather than self-ownership.

Romans connects Christ's dying and living with His lordship over dead and living. Peter's speech describes God raising Jesus and appointing Him judge of living and dead. The titles Lord and judge and the two formulations remain distinct.

Both say that all will face the judgment seat. The pinned Romans text calls it God's judgment seat; Corinthians calls it Christ's and specifies receiving what is due for bodily deeds. The names are preserved rather than normalized.

The written saying about every knee bending and every tongue confessing to God is found in Isaiah's divine oath. Romans introduces it with the Lord's living oath formula rather than reproducing Isaiah's opening 'By Myself I swear'.

Both speak of giving an account before divine judgment. Romans applies the statement to each of us before God; Peter's immediate subjects are people slandering believers, who must answer to the One judging living and dead.

Both warn against placing a stumbling block before another believer in the setting of food choices. Corinthians specifically warns that one's authority may become a stumbling block to the weak; Romans redirects judgment toward avoiding such harm.

Romans distinguishes food's uncleanness from the person's reckoning it unclean. Corinthians describes a weak conscience defiled while eating food as idol-associated. Both consider the eater's religious understanding, without importing Corinthians's stated idol background into Romans.

Both warn that a brother for whom Christ died can be destroyed through another believer's use of food or knowledge. Corinthians further calls striking the weak conscience a sin against Christ; Romans contrasts the harmful choice with walking in love.

Both discuss being spoken against in the food-and-conscience setting. Romans warns against letting one's good be spoken of as evil; Corinthians asks why freedom is judged by another conscience and thankful participation is slandered.

Both associate joy and peace with the Spirit. Romans describes the kingdom through righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit rather than eating and drinking; Galatians includes joy and peace in the fruit of the Spirit.

Both coordinate conduct before God and people: serving Christ in the stated way is pleasing to God and approved by people, while the collection administrators take care for what is honorable before both Lord and people. The immediate activities differ.

Both prioritize building others up in the context of food liberty. Corinthians distinguishes permission from what builds up and commands seeking the other's good; Romans urges pursuit of peace and mutual building.

Romans warns against tearing down God's work for food and distinguishes cleanness from eating with stumbling. Corinthians likewise describes food-related freedom and knowledge that can become a stumbling block and destroy a weak brother.

Both favor foregoing food rather than causing a brother to stumble. Corinthians states Paul's resolve never to eat meat if food causes that harm; Romans explicitly also names wine and anything else that makes the brother stumble.

The blessing of not judging oneself in what one approves is followed by the opposite case: a doubting eater is condemned because the eating is not from faith. This is an internal contrast between stated convictions and outcomes in the same food discussion.

Both make faith necessary for conduct acceptable to God. Romans's immediate example is a doubting eater; Hebrews speaks of approaching God in belief that He exists and rewards seekers. The comparison preserves these different applications of faith.

Both direct the community to support people described as weak. Romans tells the strong to bear others' weaknesses rather than please themselves; Thessalonians includes holding fast to the weak among its instructions for patient pastoral care.

Both commend pleasing others for their good rather than one's own advantage. Romans names the neighbor's building up; Corinthians describes Paul's seeking the many's benefit so that they may be saved.

Romans quotes the Psalm's clause about the reproaches of those reproaching God falling on the speaker. Paul applies that clause to Christ as the example of not pleasing Himself; the source is the actual Greek-numbered Psalm68.

Both explain that earlier scriptural material was written for present believers' instruction. Romans emphasizes perseverance, encouragement and hope; Corinthians calls the wilderness events examples written to admonish those at the ends of the ages.

Both connect shared-mindedness with Christ Jesus and care beyond oneself. Romans prays that God grant this mind among believers; Philippians exhorts the community to the same mind, humility and attention to others' interests.

Romans prays for believers with one mouth to glorify the God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ. Philippians describes every tongue confessing Jesus Christ as Lord to God the Father's glory. Spoken praise and the Father-Christ relation are shared, with different scope.

God's welcome of the eater previously grounds the prohibition of contempt and judgment. The present conclusion makes Christ's welcome of the recipients the model for welcoming one another. This is the letter's own development of the welcome argument.

Both join God's Servant with the covenant promises given to the fathers and a first address to Israel. Peter names the covenant with Abraham and says God sent His Servant first to the hearers; Romans names service to the circumcision confirming the fathers' promises.

The saying about thanking God among the nations and singing to His name is quoted from this Greek-numbered Psalm. Romans places that praise in its explanation of the Gentiles glorifying God for mercy.

Romans quotes the nations' rejoicing with God's people from the longer song stanza. The actual Deuteronomy unit also names heavens, sons of God, angels and recompense; only its nations-with-His-people clause is reproduced here.
The call for all nations and all peoples to praise the Lord is the opening of the actual Greek-numbered Psalm116. Romans cites that short summons in the sequence about Gentile praise.

The cited Jesse-root saying closely follows the actual Isaiah text: one rising to rule nations and nations hoping in him. Isaiah also describes his rest as honor; the Romans quotation centers on rule and Gentile hope.

The earlier kingdom description joins peace, joy and the Holy Spirit. The present prayer asks God to fill believers with joy and peace in believing and to give abounding hope in the Spirit's power. The recurring cluster connects kingdom life and the closing prayer.

Both describe believers' capacity or duty to admonish one another with understanding. Romans commends the recipients' goodness and knowledge; Colossians connects mutual teaching and admonition in wisdom with the richly indwelling word of Christ.

Romans grounds Paul's bold reminder in grace given by God. Galatians explicitly describes the recognized grace given to Paul and his commission among the nations, alongside Peter's work among the circumcised. This supports the stated grace-and-commission basis, not the particular wording of the reminder.

Romans describes the Gentile offering as acceptable and sanctified in the Holy Spirit. Peter reports God giving Gentiles the Spirit and cleansing their hearts by faith. Both connect Gentile acceptance with God's action, while only Romans uses the priestly offering image.

Paul's boasting in Christ Jesus concerning God's things corresponds to the instruction that the one who boasts should boast in the Lord. Both place appropriate boasting in relation to divine agency rather than mere self-commendation.

Both credit Paul's apostolic labor to divine action. Romans speaks of what Christ worked through him for Gentile obedience in word and deed; Corinthians describes his abundant labor as God's grace with him rather than himself alone.

Romans describes signs and wonders in Paul's ministry through the Spirit of God's power. Acts records Barnabas and Paul's report of signs and wonders God did among Gentiles through them. The joint report does not supply Romans's full Jerusalem-to-Illyricum geography.

Both describe Paul's aim to proclaim beyond work already established by others. Romans uses another person's foundation and Christ not yet being named; Corinthians speaks of others' labors and another's sphere over things already prepared.

Romans cites Isaiah's two linked outcomes: those to whom he was not proclaimed will see, and those who have not heard will understand. The actual Greek-based Isaiah also describes nations marveling and kings closing their mouths; the quotation selects the final clauses.

The letter's introduction says Paul often planned to come but had been hindered. The present passage repeats that delay after describing his pioneer proclamation, linking the postponed Roman visit with the argument just given.

Both speak of Paul's longing to see the Roman believers. The later statement adds the many years of longing and his present assessment of remaining place in the regions; the opening names the wish to strengthen them.

Both letters describe a planned congregational visit and the recipients' help in sending Paul onward. Romans hopes for passage toward Spain and time in their company; Corinthians describes travel through Macedonia and a possible longer stay. These are different stated plans, not proof of a completed Spanish visit.

Romans announces Paul's travel to Jerusalem to serve the saints. In his defense Paul says he came with alms for his nation and offerings and was found purified in the temple. The passages connect Jerusalem travel and charitable or religious service without equating every offering or recipient.

Romans names Macedonia among the willing contributors to the poor saints in Jerusalem. Corinthians describes Macedonian Churches' chosen generosity and earnest request to share in ministry to the saints. The target does not itself name Jerusalem or Achaia.

The collection instruction explicitly names ministry to the saints and Achaia's readiness, which Paul had praised to Macedonians. Romans names both Achaia and Macedonia as willing contributors; the Macedonians' role in these target verses is hearing that praise.

Both argue that receiving spiritual benefits appropriately leads to material support. Romans applies this to Gentile debt toward the saints whose spiritual things they shared; Corinthians applies sowing spiritual things and reaping material things to apostolic ministry.

The Spain-via-the-recipients plan is repeated after the intervening explanation of Jerusalem service. The present statement adds completing the task and sealing its fruit before departure. Both passages express intention rather than narrating fulfillment.

Both anticipate a spiritually beneficial Roman visit. The opening speaks of a shared spiritual gift and mutual encouragement through faith; the present statement expects the fullness of Christ's blessing when Paul comes.

Both call on the receiving Church's prayers as cooperation with Paul amid danger. Corinthians connects their prayer-help with God's deliverance from death; Romans urges them to struggle together with him in prayers, followed by the particular requests about Judea and Jerusalem service.

Both requests seek prayer for rescue from hostile people. Romans specifies the disobedient in Judea and adds acceptance of his service by the saints; Thessalonians asks rescue from perverse and evil people and states that not all have faith. The groups are not identified as the same people.

Both hopes for coming to Rome are explicitly conditioned by God's will and expect shared benefit with the recipients. The opening names mutual encouragement through faith; the closing request names joy and resting together.
Both use the God-of-peace-with-you blessing. Philippians connects that assurance with practicing what the recipients learned, received, heard and saw; Romans gives the short blessing to all.

Phoebe is designated a deacon of the Church in Cenchreae. Philippians addresses saints in Philippi together with overseers and deacons. The comparison follows the explicit deacon designation in different local Churches.

Both commend welcoming a servant in the Lord with honor because of service associated with Paul. Phoebe is a patron of many and Paul and is to receive needed assistance; Epaphroditus is to be welcomed with joy and honored for costly service.

The same named couple, Prisca and Aquila, appears in both Pauline greetings. Romans asks the recipients to greet Paul's fellow workers; Corinthians conveys the couple's greeting together with the Church in their house.

Both commend costly service involving risk to life. Prisca and Aquila risked their neck for Paul's life; Epaphroditus risked his own life in the work of Christ to supply service to Paul. The passages do not identify the dangers as one episode.

Both explicitly associate the Church in their house with Aquila and Prisca, the antecedent couple in Romans16:3–4. The correspondence is the named couple and house-Church association; an unchanged physical location is not asserted.

Both apply the firstfruits designation with a named region to Christian adherents. Romans names Epaenetus as Asia's firstfruits for Christ; Corinthians names Stephanas's household as Achaia's firstfruits. The people, individual-versus-household scope and regions remain distinct.

Mary's specific commendation for much labor for the recipients is paralleled by Persis's much labor in the Lord, alongside Tryphaena and Tryphosa's labor. This compares the repeated commendation within one greeting list, without merging the named people or inventing their particular tasks.

Romans names Andronicus and Junia as Paul's fellow prisoners; Colossians gives that explicit relationship to Aristarchus. The shared relationship is compared while leaving the people and any particular imprisonment episode distinct.

The greeting explicitly calls Urbanus our fellow worker in Christ, paralleling the earlier designation of Prisca and Aquila as Paul's fellow workers in Christ Jesus. This is an internal comparison of named ministry relationships; Stachys's separate beloved designation does not identify him with another person.

Paul commends Tryphaena and Tryphosa's labor in the Lord and Persis's much labor in the Lord. The earlier greeting commends Mary's much labor for the recipients. The repeated commendation connects these different named servants without assigning a shared office or task.

Both Pauline closings instruct the recipients to greet one another with a holy kiss and convey greetings from the Christian community. Romans speaks of all Churches of Christ; Corinthians speaks of all the brothers.

Both direct withdrawal from people causing division. Romans names divisions and snares contrary to learned teaching; Titus specifies having nothing further to do with a divisive person after first and second warnings. Its stated warning procedure is not inserted into Romans.

Both oppose allegiance to Christ to the belly image for corrupt motives. Romans says the deceivers serve their own belly rather than the Lord Christ; Philippians describes enemies of Christ's cross whose god is the belly. The target does not repeat the smooth-speech description.

Both combine mature discernment with innocence toward evil. Romans wants wisdom about good and innocence about evil; Corinthians commands maturity in thinking and infancy in evil. The passages distinguish understanding from participation in wrongdoing.

Both connect overcoming Satan or the enemy with underfoot imagery and divine action. Romans promises the God of peace will crush Satan under the recipients' feet; Jesus describes seeing Satan fall and giving the disciples authority to tread on snakes and scorpions and over the enemy's power.

Timothy's named partnership with Paul is explicit in both letters: fellow worker here and one who served with Paul for the gospel in Philippians. This anchors Timothy's ministry relationship; it does not identify Lucius, Jason or Sosipater with similarly named people elsewhere.

Both Pauline letters explicitly identify a writing hand. Romans has Tertius say he wrote the letter; Corinthians marks the greeting as Paul's own hand. The comparison distinguishes those stated hands and does not attribute the Corinthian body to Tertius.

Gaius is called Paul's host and host of the whole Church. Lydia urges Paul's company to enter her house and stay. These are different named examples of hospitality supporting the mission; the comparison does not identify Gaius with another bearer of that name.

Both give the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ to all the recipients as a closing blessing. The Romans unit's original double brackets are retained; the comparison is with the actual Thessalonian formula, without importing its textual status.

The Romans doxology's revealed mystery, kept silent through long ages and continued as now revealed in16:26, parallels the mystery hidden through ages and generations but now revealed to the saints in Colossians. Colossians locates the riches of this mystery among the nations and identifies the mystery as Christ in you, the hope of glory.

The closing doxology repeats the distinctive purpose of the obedience of faith among all the nations found in the opening account of grace and apostleship. The current continuation also names prophetic writings and the eternal God's command, completing the letter's mission frame.

Both give glory to the only God through Jesus Christ and close with the ages and Amen. Romans calls God wise; Jude calls Him Savior and adds majesty, might and authority. Wise is not inserted into Jude's actual wording.

deferred.reason: Ampliatus is greeted as beloved in the Lord, with no further act, role or securely matched identity stated. A link based only on the common beloved greeting would be too general to retain.

Apelles's approved-in-Christ description and the greeting to Aristobulus's household do not establish a particular shared episode or identity elsewhere. The separately read household greeting in2Timothy4:19 supplies a formula, not a specific connection for these people.

Herodion's kinship label and the believing members of Narcissus's household are retained exactly. No particular degree of kinship, identity with a Herod, belief of Narcissus himself or matched household history is established by the greeting.

The repeated Rufus name inMark15:21 does not establish identity with Simon's son. The mother-and-mine phrase is unexplained here; the general familial instruction in1Timothy5:1–2 does not determine this particular relationship, so no biographical identification is retained.

The list names these people and the brothers with them but no specific event or task. The Hermes label assigned to Paul by the crowd inActs14:12 is not an identity for this named Christian; a shared name or general greeting is insufficient.

The greeting names Philologus, Julia, Nereus and his unnamed sister, Olympas and the saints with them. No specific matching episode or identity was found to retain; spouse relationships, the sister's name and a particular meeting place must not be invented.
